claim: Many organisms—from bacteria to nematodes to insect larvae—navigate their environments by biasing random movements.
source: Many organisms—from bacteria to nematodes to insect larvae—navigate their environments by biasing random movements.
evidence: This is a general statement about organism navigation that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In isotropic environments, navigation can be characterized as an essentially diffusive and undirected process.
source: In these organisms, navigation in isotropic environments can be characterized as an essentially diffusive and undirected process.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and analysis presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 1.

claim: In stimulus gradients, movement decisions are biased to drive directed navigation toward favorable environments.
source: In stimulus gradients, movement decisions are biased to drive directed navigation toward favorable environments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3, and draws from established knowledge in the field.

claim: The statistics of random exploration in any direction are little affected by directed movement along a stimulus gradient.
source: We find that the statistics of random exploration in any direction are little affected by directed movement along a stimulus gradient.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the diffusion analysis presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: A key constraint on the behavioral strategies of these organisms appears to be the preservation of their capacity to continuously explore their environments in all directions even while moving toward favorable conditions.
source: A key constraint on the behavioral strategies of these organisms appears to be the preservation of their capacity to continuously explore their environments in all directions even while moving toward favorable conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The swimming behavior of Escherichia coli is characterized by an alternating sequence of runs and tumbles.
source: A classic example is the swimming behavior of Escherichia coli (; Berg, 1993), which is characterized by an alternating sequence of runs and tumbles.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berg, 1993.

claim: During runs, bacteria swim in roughly straight lines.
source: During runs, the bacteria swim in roughly straight lines, while during tumbles, the bacteria move erratically in place, ultimately picking the direction of a new run at random.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial behavior, supported by the citation to Berg, 1993.

claim: During tumbles, bacteria move erratically in place and pick the direction of a new run at random.
source: During runs, the bacteria swim in roughly straight lines, while during tumbles, the bacteria move erratically in place, ultimately picking the direction of a new run at random.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial behavior, supported by the citation to Berg, 1993.

claim: The trajectories of larger animals like nematodes and insect larvae are qualitatively similar to bacterial trajectories.
source: The trajectories of larger animals like nematodes and insect larvae are qualitatively similar (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999; Luo et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999 and Luo et al., 2010.

claim: Caenorhabditis elegans alternate periods of forward movement with either large angle reorientation maneuvers called pirouettes or small angle turns.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans alternate periods of forward movement with either large angle reorientation maneuvers called pirouettes or small angle turns.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans behavior, supported by the preceding citation to Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999.

claim: Crawling Drosophila larvae alternate periods of forward movement with turns where they pause forward motion and use the angle of head swings to pick a new forward orientation.
source: Crawling Drosophila larvae alternate periods of forward movement with turns (Lahiri et al., 2011) where they pause forward motion and use the angle of head swings to pick a new forward orientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lahiri et al., 2011.

claim: C. elegans modulates its random exploration in isotropic environments over time.
source: C. elegans also modulates its random exploration in isotropic environments over time (Wakabayashi et al., 2004; Chalasani et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wakabayashi et al., 2004 and Chalasani et al., 2007.

claim: When a worm is placed in a new environment, it first executes a local search, where runs are short.
source: When a worm is placed in a new environment, it first executes a local search, where runs are short.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the preceding citations to Wakabayashi et al., 2004 and Chalasani et al., 2007.

claim: Over time, worms transition to a global search with longer runs.
source: Over time, worms transition to a global search with longer runs.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the preceding citations to Wakabayashi et al., 2004 and Chalasani et al., 2007.

claim: It has been suggested that the transition between local and global searching is discontinuous.
source: It has been suggested that the transition between local and global searching is discontinuous (Calhoun et al., 2014), and that local search and global search represent two distinct behavioral states.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Calhoun et al., 2014.

claim: Local search and global search represent two distinct behavioral states.
source: It has been suggested that the transition between local and global searching is discontinuous (Calhoun et al., 2014), and that local search and global search represent two distinct behavioral states.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Calhoun et al., 2014.

claim: Bacteria, nematodes, and insect larvae bias their random walks toward favorable environments by modulating the statistics of transitions between forward-moving runs and reorientation events.
source: In stimulus gradients, bacteria, nematodes, and insect larvae bias their random walks toward favorable environments by modulating the statistics of transitions between forward-moving runs and reorientation events.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field and is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All three organisms exhibit longer runs when pointed toward favorable conditions.
source: For example, all three organisms exhibit longer runs when pointed toward favorable conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field and is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Worms and larvae augment the time spent pointed toward favorable directions by increasing the probability of ending reorientation events with a run pointed in a favorable direction or by gradually steering runs toward favorable directions.
source: Worms and larvae further augment the time spent pointed toward favorable directions by increasing the probability of ending reorientation events with a run pointed in a favorable direction or by gradually steering runs toward favorable directions.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field and is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The navigational dynamics of worms and larvae have parallels with the complex dynamics of a polypeptide chain navigating to the native structure of the protein.
source: The navigational dynamics of worms and larvae have some parallels with the complex dynamics of a polypeptide chain navigating to the native structure of the protein to which it corresponds.
evidence: This is an inference and conceptual framework proposed by the authors.

claim: Both protein folding and organism navigation are examples of stochastic search processes.
source: Both are examples of stochastic search processes: the protein needs to fold to the correct native structure, while an organism needs to find food and favorable temperatures, for example.
evidence: This is an inference and conceptual framework proposed by the authors.

claim: A purely random search would lead to the Levinthal paradox for protein folding.
source: For the protein folding case, it would lead to the Levinthal paradox; that is, it would take an essentially infinite amount of time to fold, while in fact it takes on the order of seconds to minutes (Zwanzig et al., 1992; Karplus, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zwanzig et al., 1992 and Karplus, 1997.

claim: Protein folding takes on the order of seconds to minutes.
source: For the protein folding case, it would lead to the Levinthal paradox; that is, it would take an essentially infinite amount of time to fold, while in fact it takes on the order of seconds to minutes (Zwanzig et al., 1992; Karplus, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zwanzig et al., 1992 and Karplus, 1997.

claim: The stochastic search of a protein is biased toward the native structure by the potential energy, which is encoded in the sequence as the result of evolutionary selection.
source: The stochastic search of a protein is biased toward the native structure by the potential energy, which is encoded in the sequence as the result of evolutionary selection.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of protein folding.

claim: The stochastic component of the biased search is necessary to avoid being trapped in local minima on the potential energy surface.
source: The stochastic component of the biased search is necessary to avoid being trapped in local minima on the potential energy surface.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of protein folding.

claim: Trapping in metastable states has been observed in protein folding trajectories.
source: Trapping in such metastable states has been observed in protein folding trajectories, where an escape is made possible only by the stochastic nature of the dynamics.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of protein folding.

claim: A purely random search would be very inefficient for organism navigation due to the large size of the space accessible in their normal environment.
source: A purely random search would by very inefficient due to the large size of the space accessible in their normal environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on general principles of search efficiency.

claim: Living organisms use cues to bias their search.
source: Thus, living organisms use cues to bias their search.
evidence: This is established knowledge and is supported by the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: A temperature gradient plays the role of the potential energy in organism navigation.
source: An example is a temperature gradient which plays the role of the potential energy.
evidence: This is an inference and conceptual framework proposed by the authors.

claim: A purely deterministic search would not be effective for organism navigation because there can be traps (local minima) in the accessible space.
source: A purely deterministic search would not be effective here either, because there can be traps (local minima) in the accessible space.
evidence: This is an inference based on general principles of search efficiency.

claim: A stochastic component in the biased search allows organisms to overcome the trapping problem.
source: A stochastic component in the biased search allows the organisms to overcome the trapping problem.
evidence: This is an inference based on general principles of search efficiency.

claim: The actual details of the navigational dynamics are specified by the neural circuitry that enervates the muscles.
source: The actual details of the navigational dynamics are specified by the neural circuitry that enervates the muscles.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience and behavioral biology.

claim: The neural circuitry is optimized by evolution, in analogy to the amino acid sequence in proteins.
source: This is optimized by evolution, in analogy to the amino acid sequence in proteins.
evidence: This is an inference and conceptual framework proposed by the authors.

claim: Folding dynamics can be quantitatively described as diffusion (random walk) on a free-energy landscape.
source: The folding dynamics can be quantitatively described as diffusion (random walk) on a free-energy landscape.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of protein folding.

claim: The free-energy barrier between unfolded and folded states defines the bottleneck of the folding reaction.
source: The free-energy barrier between unfolded and folded states defines the bottleneck of the folding reaction.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of protein folding.

claim: The diffusion coefficient describes how quickly the system explores the configuration space.
source: The diffusion coefficient describes how quickly the system—whether a worm, larvae, or peptide sequence—explores the configuration space.
evidence: This is established knowledge in statistical mechanics and the conceptual framework proposed by the authors.

claim: The free-energy barrier and the diffusion coefficient together determine the rate of the process.
source: Together, the free-energy barrier and the diffusion coefficient determine the rate of the process.
evidence: This is established knowledge in statistical mechanics and chemical kinetics.

claim: The free-energy landscape framework is generic and has been successfully applied to many different types of complex dynamics.
source: We note also that the free-energy landscape framework is generic and has been successfully applied to many different types of complex dynamics, for example, the dynamics of the game of chess (Krivov, 2011b) or patient recovery dynamics after kidney transplant (Krivov et al., 2014), as well as to protein folding.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krivov, 2011b and Krivov et al., 2014.

claim: The free-energy landscape framework has been applied to the dynamics of the game of chess.
source: We note also that the free-energy landscape framework is generic and has been successfully applied to many different types of complex dynamics, for example, the dynamics of the game of chess (Krivov, 2011b) or patient recovery dynamics after kidney transplant (Krivov et al., 2014), as well as to protein folding.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krivov, 2011b.

claim: The free-energy landscape framework has been applied to patient recovery dynamics after kidney transplant.
source: We note also that the free-energy landscape framework is generic and has been successfully applied to many different types of complex dynamics, for example, the dynamics of the game of chess (Krivov, 2011b) or patient recovery dynamics after kidney transplant (Krivov et al., 2014), as well as to protein folding.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krivov et al., 2014.

claim: There are many variants of detailed motions which are likely to result in very similar larger scale navigational dynamics.
source: However, there are many variants of detailed motions, which are likely to result in very similar larger scale navigational dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conceptual framework proposed by the authors.

claim: It is the invariants of large-scale dynamics that are expected to be optimized by evolution.
source: Thus, it is of interest to understand and accurately characterize the invariants of large-scale dynamics. It is precisely these invariants that are expected to be optimized by evolution.
evidence: This is an inference and speculation based on evolutionary principles.

claim: A description using the free-energy landscape framework can provide an intuitive picture of the complex navigational dynamics as a whole.
source: Moreover, a description making use of the free-energy landscape framework can provide an intuitive picture of the complex navigational dynamics as a whole, versus the localized description of dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conceptual framework proposed by the authors.

claim: The free-energy landscape framework could be used to locate equilibrium populations, biases, and bottlenecks during navigation toward the target in complex environments.
source: It could be used, in particular, to locate equilibrium populations, biases, and bottlenecks during the navigation toward the target in complex environments.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the framework.

claim: The free-energy landscape of a protein can be determined from long equilibrium trajectories.
source: The free-energy landscape of a protein can be determined from long equilibrium trajectories (Krivov and Karplus, 2004; Krivov, 2011a; Banushkina and Krivov, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krivov and Karplus, 2004; Krivov, 2011a; and Banushkina and Krivov, 2016.

claim: The experimental trajectories of crawling animals are too short to be considered to be at equilibrium in comparison with those in the reversible folding/unfolding of proteins at equilibrium.
source: However, the experimental trajectories of the crawling animals treated here are too short to be considered to be at equilibrium in comparison with those in the reversible folding/unfolding of proteins at equilibrium (Shaw et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with protein folding studies, supported by a citation to Shaw et al., 2010.

claim: The Markov state model exploits the information contained in a large number of short trajectories measured under identical conditions.
source: To determine the equilibrium properties, which are required for the construction of the free-energy landscape, we introduce another general approach to random dynamics, the Markov state model (MSM). This exploits the information contained in a large number of short trajectories measured under identical conditions (Lane et al., 2011; Rao and Caflisch, 2004; Krivov et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lane et al., 2011; Rao and Caflisch, 2004; and Krivov et al., 2002.

claim: Dynamics are Markovian if the next crawling step of an animal depends only on its current spatial position.
source: One refers to the dynamics as Markovian if the next crawling step of an animal depends only on its current spatial position; that is, it quickly forgets the history of its motion.
evidence: This is a definition of Markovian dynamics.

claim: A collection of short trajectories can be used to determine a probability distribution of future positions of the animal starting from a current position.
source: A collection of short trajectories can then be used to determine a probability distribution of future positions of the animal starting from a current position.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the Markov state model approach.

claim: The steady state probability distribution can be determined from a collection of short trajectories.
source: In particular, the steady state probability distribution can be determined in this way.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the Markov state model approach.

claim: The steady state distribution is the equilibrium distribution for the worms.
source: The analysis is based on the construction of the transition probability matrix, as described in Materials and methods, where it is shown that the steady state distribution is, in fact, the equilibrium distribution for the worms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The transition probability matrix provides a complete description of the stochastic dynamics.
source: This matrix provides a complete description of the stochastic dynamics and can be used to determine long time scale behavior.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the Markov state model approach.

claim: Worms placed at their cultivation temperature do not strictly avoid warmer temperatures.
source: The analysis of a large number of trajectories with the MSM showed that worms do not strictly avoid warmer temperatures, potentially uncovering a different interpretation of isothermal tracking behavior (see Results section).
evidence: This is a finding from the MSM analysis presented in the Results section, specifically Figure 4.

claim: C. elegans and Drosophila larvae trajectories exhibit diffusive behavior under isotropic conditions.
source: These trajectories (Figure 1A,A') do exhibit diffusive behavior, but do not demonstrate active movement in a particular direction, as demonstrated by their very small values for the dimensionless drift velocity (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of trajectories under isotropic conditions, supported by Figure 1.

claim: C. elegans and Drosophila larvae do not demonstrate active movement in a particular direction under isotropic conditions.
source: These trajectories (Figure 1A,A') do exhibit diffusive behavior, but do not demonstrate active movement in a particular direction, as demonstrated by their very small values for the dimensionless drift velocity (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of trajectories under isotropic conditions, supported by Figure 1.

claim: C. elegans crawling under isotropic conditions drastically reduce their turning rate throughout an experiment.
source: C. elegans crawling under isotropic conditions drastically reduce their turning rate (i.e. make longer runs) throughout an experiment (Figure 1B), as also noted in previous work (Calhoun et al., 2014); here, it is studied over a substantially longer time of ~1 hr.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of C. elegans behavior under isotropic conditions, supported by Figure 1B and a citation to Calhoun et al., 2014.

claim: The turning rate of C. elegans under isotropic conditions decreases exponentially with a time constant of approximately 800 s.
source: In particular, the turning rate decreases exponentially with a time constant of approximately 800 s (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of C. elegans behavior under isotropic conditions, supported by Figure 1B.

claim: Individual C. elegans trajectories do not show strong evidence of the turning rate undergoing an abrupt transition from local to global searching.
source: Inspecting the run durations for individual worm trajectories (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we do not see strong evidence of the turning rate undergoing an abrupt transition from local to global searching, but rather a regular decline, which in the population averages to steady exponential decay.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of individual C. elegans trajectories, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: C. elegans turning rate shows a regular decline which in the population averages to steady exponential decay.
source: Inspecting the run durations for individual worm trajectories (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we do not see strong evidence of the turning rate undergoing an abrupt transition from local to global searching, but rather a regular decline, which in the population averages to steady exponential decay.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of C. elegans trajectories, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Frequent turns within a random walk will reduce the diffusion rate.
source: Turning rate has a clear connection to the dynamics, as frequent turns within a random walk will reduce the diffusion rate.
evidence: This is an inference based on general principles of random walk dynamics.

claim: For C. elegans under isotropic conditions, diffusion coefficients converge to different limiting values in the first and second halves of experiments.
source: As expected, the diffusion coefficients converge to different limiting values, with diffusion during the second part of the experiments nearly double that during the first part.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of C. elegans behavior under isotropic conditions, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: For C. elegans under isotropic conditions, diffusion during the second part of experiments is nearly double that during the first part.
source: As expected, the diffusion coefficients converge to different limiting values, with diffusion during the second part of the experiments nearly double that during the first part.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of C. elegans behavior under isotropic conditions, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: Drosophila larvae under isotropic conditions exhibit similar behavior to C. elegans in terms of trajectory structure.
source: Drosophila larvae under isotropic conditions (Figure 1A'–C') exhibit similar behavior in terms of trajectory structure (Figure 1A') and the transition to a diffusive regime, but they do not exhibit a marked decline in turning rate (Figure 1B'), which stabilizes after only a few minutes and remains constant throughout their searching behavior.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of Drosophila larvae behavior under isotropic conditions, supported by Figure 1A'.

claim: Drosophila larvae under isotropic conditions do not exhibit a marked decline in turning rate.
source: Drosophila larvae under isotropic conditions (Figure 1A'–C') exhibit similar behavior in terms of trajectory structure (Figure 1A') and the transition to a diffusive regime, but they do not exhibit a marked decline in turning rate (Figure 1B'), which stabilizes after only a few minutes and remains constant throughout their searching behavior.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of Drosophila larvae behavior under isotropic conditions, supported by Figure 1B'.

claim: Drosophila larvae turning rate stabilizes after only a few minutes and remains constant throughout their searching behavior under isotropic conditions.
source: Drosophila larvae under isotropic conditions (Figure 1A'–C') exhibit similar behavior in terms of trajectory structure (Figure 1A') and the transition to a diffusive regime, but they do not exhibit a marked decline in turning rate (Figure 1B'), which stabilizes after only a few minutes and remains constant throughout their searching behavior.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of Drosophila larvae behavior under isotropic conditions, supported by Figure 1B'.

claim: The transition from local to global searching does not appear on the ~15-min time scales measured for Drosophila larva behavior.
source: Thus, the transition from local to global searching does not appear on the ~15-min time scales we measured for larva behavior.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of Drosophila larvae behavior under isotropic conditions.

claim: Worms cultivated at 15°C and placed in a gradient centered at 20°C exhibited negative thermotaxis.
source: Worms cultivated at 15°C and placed in a gradient centered at 20°C exhibited negative thermotaxis (also called 'cryophilic' behavior), while larvae placed at 17.5°C in the same gradient crawled away from cold conditions, exhibiting positive thermotaxis to a preferred range that is independent of cultivation conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the thermotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 2A.

claim: Drosophila larvae placed at 17.5°C in a temperature gradient crawled away from cold conditions, exhibiting positive thermotaxis.
source: Worms cultivated at 15°C and placed in a gradient centered at 20°C exhibited negative thermotaxis (also called 'cryophilic' behavior), while larvae placed at 17.5°C in the same gradient crawled away from cold conditions, exhibiting positive thermotaxis to a preferred range that is independent of cultivation conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the thermotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 2A.

claim: Drosophila larvae exhibit positive thermotaxis to a preferred range that is independent of cultivation conditions.
source: Worms cultivated at 15°C and placed in a gradient centered at 20°C exhibited negative thermotaxis (also called 'cryophilic' behavior), while larvae placed at 17.5°C in the same gradient crawled away from cold conditions, exhibiting positive thermotaxis to a preferred range that is independent of cultivation conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the thermotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 2A.

claim: Navigation does not eliminate stochasticity along the axis of purposeful navigation.
source: This suggests that navigation does not eliminate stochasticity along the axis of purposeful navigation.
evidence: This is an inference from the diffusion analysis during thermotaxis.

claim: Animals conduct a random search in all directions irrespective of whether they have adopted a target direction.
source: That is, the animals conduct a random search in all directions irrespective of whether they have adopted a target direction.
evidence: This is an inference from the diffusion analysis during thermotaxis.

claim: There is a tradeoff between searching along an axis and purposeful travel in that direction.
source: This suggests that there is a tradeoff between searching along an axis and purposeful travel in that direction.
evidence: This is an inference from the diffusion analysis during thermotaxis.

claim: Worms undergoing negative thermotaxis reorient their crawling direction more frequently when heading up the temperature gradient.
source: For example, worms undergoing negative thermotaxis reorient their crawling direction more frequently when heading up the temperature gradient, and maintain longer runs when heading down the gradient (Figure 2B, lower right).
evidence: This is a finding from the thermotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Worms undergoing negative thermotaxis maintain longer runs when heading down the temperature gradient.
source: For example, worms undergoing negative thermotaxis reorient their crawling direction more frequently when heading up the temperature gradient, and maintain longer runs when heading down the gradient (Figure 2B, lower right).
evidence: This is a finding from the thermotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Thermotaxing Drosophila larvae have a higher turning rate when crawling toward aversive colder conditions.
source: Thermotaxing larvae, similarly, have a higher turning rate when crawling toward aversive colder conditions, and maintain longer runs crawling up the gradient (Figure 2B', lower right).
evidence: This is a finding from the thermotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 2B'.

claim: Thermotaxing Drosophila larvae maintain longer runs crawling up the temperature gradient.
source: Thermotaxing larvae, similarly, have a higher turning rate when crawling toward aversive colder conditions, and maintain longer runs crawling up the gradient (Figure 2B', lower right).
evidence: This is a finding from the thermotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 2B'.

claim: During thermotaxis, worms decrease their turning rate over time.
source: As was true for isotropic conditions, worms decrease their turning rate over time (and larvae maintain a stable level).
evidence: This is a finding from the thermotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 2B.

claim: During thermotaxis, Drosophila larvae maintain a stable turning rate level.
source: As was true for isotropic conditions, worms decrease their turning rate over time (and larvae maintain a stable level).
evidence: This is a finding from the thermotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 2B'.

claim: During thermotaxis, both C. elegans and Drosophila larvae maintain an approximately constant ratio between toward-warm turning rates and toward-cold turning rates.
source: However, both animals maintain an approximately constant ratio between toward-warm turning rates and toward-cold turning rates.
evidence: This is a finding from the thermotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 2B,B'.

claim: The primary navigational bias that produces thermotaxis is not altered at long time scales.
source: That is, the primary navigational bias that produces thermotaxis is not altered, even at long time scales.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of turning rate ratios during thermotaxis.

claim: The constancy of the turning rate ratio supports the method of using early behavior to model long term behavior.
source: Importantly, this supports the method of using early behavior to model long term behavior.
evidence: This is an inference about the validity of the methodological approach.

claim: C. elegans chemotax either up or down salt gradients, depending on the baseline salt level.
source: Worms chemotax either up or down salt gradients, depending on the baseline salt level (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the chemotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: At low baseline salt concentrations (25 mM), C. elegans move toward higher salt levels.
source: At low baseline salt concentrations (25 mM), worms move toward higher salt levels, and at high concentrations (75 mM) they crawl down the gradient toward lower salt levels.
evidence: This is a finding from the chemotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: At high salt concentrations (75 mM), C. elegans crawl down the gradient toward lower salt levels.
source: At low baseline salt concentrations (25 mM), worms move toward higher salt levels, and at high concentrations (75 mM) they crawl down the gradient toward lower salt levels.
evidence: This is a finding from the chemotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: During chemotaxis, C. elegans behavior converges to diffusive behavior at longer times.
source: As with thermal navigation, worm behavior converges to diffusive behavior at longer times (Figure 3B), and local searching transitions gradually to global searching via a reduced turning rate (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the chemotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: During chemotaxis, C. elegans local searching transitions gradually to global searching via a reduced turning rate.
source: As with thermal navigation, worm behavior converges to diffusive behavior at longer times (Figure 3B), and local searching transitions gradually to global searching via a reduced turning rate (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the chemotaxis experiments, supported by Figure 3C.

claim: The Markov state model predicts equilibrium population distributions consistent with the net motion of the population during chemotaxis.
source: The Markov state model predicts equilibrium population distributions consistent with the net motion of the population (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from the Markov state model analysis of chemotaxis, supported by Figure 3D.

claim: The general framework of diffusion and Markov processes can be used to combine a large number of short trajectories obtained under identical conditions in both isotropic environments and in the presence of stimulus gradients.
source: Here, we have focused on diffusion along perpendicular axes, and used Markov analysis techniques to investigate the combination of exploratory diffusion and targeted navigation. We found that the general framework of diffusion and Markov processes can be used to combine a large number of short trajectories obtained under identical conditions in both isotropic environments and in the presence of stimulus gradients.
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Random exploration in all directions and across all time scales is remarkably robust to progression in a selected direction in a graded environment.
source: In both animals and across stimulus types, we found importantly that random exploration in all directions and across all time scales is remarkably robust to progression in a selected direction in a graded environment.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: When nematodes and insect larvae encounter stimuli that bias their random walks in specific directions, the effectiveness of random searching is largely unaffected either parallel or orthogonal to the direction of motion.
source: When nematodes and insect larvae encounter stimuli that bias their random walks in specific directions, the effectiveness of random searching is largely unaffected either parallel or orthogonal to the direction of motion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A constraint on the mechanisms that generate navigation in a preferred direction appears to be the preservation of the statistics of random exploration in all directions across time scales.
source: In these animals, a constraint on the mechanisms that generate navigation in a preferred direction appears to be the preservation of the statistics of random exploration in all directions across time scales.
evidence: This is an inference from the primary findings of the manuscript.

claim: Analysis of the entropy of trajectory configurations provides information that is not readily apparent in conventional metrics of drift rates and stimulus-evoked turn rates.
source: Analysis of the entropy of trajectory configurations, which avoids settling into traps, provides information that is not readily apparent in conventional metrics of drift rates and stimulus-evoked turn rates.
evidence: This is an inference about the value of the analytical approach used in the manuscript.

claim: The approach makes possible large-scale and long time descriptions of the navigational dynamics beyond those available from the standard localized run — turn — run measurements.
source: Moreover, the approach makes possible large-scale and long time descriptions of the navigational dynamics beyond those available from the standard localized run — turn — run measurements.
evidence: This is an inference about the value of the analytical approach used in the manuscript.

claim: The transition from ballistic to diffusive motion during navigation occurs over a ~1000 s time scale in both C. elegans and Drosophila larvae.
source: We found, in both animal model systems investigated here, that the transition from ballistic to diffusive motion during navigation occurs over a ~1000 s time scale, which is longer than most behavior experiments in studies of these animals.
evidence: This is a finding from the analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ~1000 s time scale for transition from ballistic to diffusive motion is longer than most behavior experiments in studies of these animals.
source: We found, in both animal model systems investigated here, that the transition from ballistic to diffusive motion during navigation occurs over a ~1000 s time scale, which is longer than most behavior experiments in studies of these animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with typical experimental durations in the field.

claim: It is possible that further behavioral transitions at longer time scales have yet to be observed.
source: Combined with the observation, in broad agreement with recent results from other experimenters (Calhoun et al., 2014), that the rate of behavioral transitions changes over time (especially in worms), it is possible that further behavioral transitions at longer time scales have yet to observed.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings and comparison with other work.

claim: Experimental techniques that enable long-time-scale measurements may be essential for uncovering a more complete picture of the behavior in these animal systems.
source: Experimental techniques that enable long-time-scale measurements may be essential for uncovering a more complete picture of the behavior in these animal systems.
evidence: This is speculation about future experimental directions.

claim: The transition to more global searching (lower turning rate) occurs at very different times in C. elegans and Drosophila larvae.
